claims.source: In OAs, acceleration had high partial R2 values (median: 0.51, CI=[0.36–0.61]), while the jerk and velocity contributions were small (median partial R2: 0.07, CI=[0.02–0.13] and 0.03, CI=[0.02–0.06], respectively).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measures of component contributions for otolith afferents.

claims.claim: In central neurons, the velocity contribution was greatest (median partial R2: 0.38), followed by acceleration and jerk (median partial R2: 0.23 and 0.14, respectively).
claims.source: In central neurons, the velocity contribution was greatest (median partial R2: 0.38, CI=[0.35–0.4]), followed by acceleration and jerk (median partial R2 : 0.23, CI=[0.21–0.25] and 0.14, CI=[0.13–0.15], respectively).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measures of component contributions for central neurons.

claims.claim: 'A' afferents had a lower normalized coefficient of variation CV* than 'AJ/VAJ' afferents (median 0.026 versus 0.06).
claims.source: In particular 'A' afferents had a lower normalized coefficient of variation CV* (Goldberg et al., 1984) than 'AJ/VAJ' afferents (median 0.026, CI=[0.024–0.033] versus 0.06, CI=[0.04–0.08], Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=10−3; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in firing regularity between afferent types.

claims.claim: The higher the CV* in otolith afferents, the higher the weights for velocity, acceleration and jerk.
claims.source: We also found that the higher the CV* the higher the weights for velocity, acceleration and jerk (WV−green, WA-red, WJ-blue; Figure 5B, Spearman's rank correlation p<10−2 for all three variables), as response gain increases with CV*.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant correlation between CV* and component weights.

claims.claim: The contribution of velocity remained minimal in otolith afferents (median = 0.06) and did not correlate with CV*.
claims.source: In contrast, the contribution of velocity remained minimal (median = 0.06, CI=[0.05–0.08]) and did not correlate with CV* (Spearman's rank correlation, p=0.75; Figure 5C, green).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of correlation between velocity contribution and CV* in otolith afferents.

claims.claim: The preferred directions of the acceleration and jerk components were always aligned for OAs with a median angular difference of 7°.
claims.source: The preferred directions for acceleration and jerk are aligned in all afferents that are tuned to these components (Figure 7D; see also Figure 5D, black).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the alignment of preferred directions for acceleration and jerk in otolith afferents.

claims.claim: The normalized acceleration weight is significantly smaller for VN and CN neurons compared to otolith afferents (p<10−8).
claims.source: Quantitatively (see Table 2), the normalized acceleration weight (Figure 6E), which is high for otolith afferents, becomes significantly smaller for VN and CN neurons (p<10−8, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in acceleration weights between afferents and central neurons.

claims.claim: The velocity weights are significantly greater for VN and CN neurons compared to otolith afferents (p<10−14).
claims.source: In parallel, the velocity weights (Figure 6D) are significantly greater for VN and CN neurons, as compared to otolith afferents (p<10−14, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in velocity weights between afferents and central neurons.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference between weight values for VN and CN areas.
claims.source: Remarkably, despite dramatic differences in the relative weighting of acceleration and velocity signals between central cells and otolith afferents, VN and CN have similar properties overall, and there is no significant difference between weight values for the two areas (Wilcoxon's rank sum test, wv: p=0.75; wa; p=0.47; wj: p=0.28).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of significant differences between VN and CN neurons.

claims.claim: Visual/vestibular multisensory areas (MSTd, VPS, VIP and FEF) have slightly greater velocity weight (median: 0.39) compared to areas without optic flow responsiveness (VN, CN, PIVC; median 0.32) (p<10−9).
claims.source: The most noticeable difference among cortical areas is the slightly greater velocity weight in visual/vestibular multisensory areas (MSTd, VPS, VIP and FEF; median: 0.39, CI=[0.38–0.41]), as compared to those without optic flow responsiveness (VN, CN, PIVC; median 0.32, CI=[0.31–0.35]) (Figure 6D, cold vs. warm colors, respectively; p<10−9, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in velocity weights between multisensory and non-multisensory areas.

claims.claim: OAs that were fit with the AJ or VAJ models have very high separability indices (median 0.98).
claims.source: OAs that were fit with the AJ or VAJ models (n = 14) generally have very high separability indices (median 0.98, CI=[0.97–0.99]), indicating that their strongest temporal components have similar preferred directions and spatial tuning.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative separability measures for otolith afferents.

claims.claim: Central brain areas have overall lower separability indices (median 0.89) compared to otolith afferents (p<10−12).
claims.source: In contrast, central brain areas have overall lower separability indices (median 0.89, CI=[0.88–0.9]; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<10−12).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in separability between afferents and central neurons.

claims.claim: There was a significant difference between the separability indices of VN/CN (median 0.82) and cortical regions (median 0.9) (p<10−8).
claims.source: Within central cells, we found a significant difference between the separability indices of VN/CN and cortical regions (median 0.82, [0.81 0.84] CI versus 0.9, [0.89 0.91] CI, Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<10−8).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in separability between subcortical and cortical neurons.

claims.claim: Otolith afferents had the smallest modulation amplitude (median = 10 spikes/s) compared to all other brain areas (median = 43 spikes/s for central neurons) (p=10−11).
claims.source: Otolith afferents had the smallest modulation amplitude (peak-to-trough amplitude of the spatio-temporal response curves, computed from the VAJ model fit) as compared to all other brain areas (median = 10 spikes/s, CI=[8-18] for OA versus 43 spikes/s, CI=[41-46] for all central neurons, Wilcoxon rank sum test: p=10−11; Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in response amplitude between afferents and central neurons.

claims.claim: VN, CN and PIVC neurons had greater aggregate modulation amplitude (median = 58 spikes/s) than visual/vestibular multisensory areas VPS, MSTd, VIP and FEF (median: 35 spikes/s) (p<10−13).
claims.source: VN, CN and PIVC neurons were the most responsive (Figure 8A, warm colors), with aggregate modulation amplitude (median = 58 spikes/s, CI=[54-63]) greater than visual/vestibular multisensory areas VPS, MSTd, VIP and FEF (Figure 8A, cold colors; median: 35 spikes/s, CI=[33-39], Wilcoxon's rank sum test: p<10−13).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in response amplitude between vestibular and multisensory areas.

claims.claim: Baseline firing rate (FR0) was greatest in otolith afferents (median = 72 spikes/s), intermediate in VN/CN (median = 45 spikes/s), and smallest in cortical areas (median = 12 spikes/s).
claims.source: FRo, which was greatest in otolith afferents (median = 72 spikes/s, CI=[54-90], Figure 8B, brown), intermediate in VN/CN (median = 45 spikes/s, CI=[38-49], Figure 8B, yellow/orange), and smallest in cortical areas (median = 12 spikes/s, CI=[11-13], Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative baseline firing rates across brain regions.

claims.claim: OAs mainly encode acceleration and jerk with cosine tuning, with offset parameters clustering around zero.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 2, OAs mainly encode acceleration and jerk with cosine tuning. Accordingly, the offset parameters of the acceleration and jerk components cluster around zero for OAs (Figure 9B,C).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the spatial tuning characteristics of otolith afferents.

claims.claim: Jerk responses in central neurons exhibited positive offsets (median 0.49) comparable to velocity responses.
claims.source: Finally, we found that jerk responses in central neurons also exhibited positive offsets (median 0.49, CI=[0.46 0.52]; Figure 9C) comparable to velocity responses.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the offset characteristics of jerk components in central neurons.

claims.claim: Many central neurons had significant position contributions: OA: 1/27 (4%), VN: 41/49 (84%), CN: 47/61 (77%), PIVC: 63/115 (55%), VPS: 51/69 (74%), MSTd: 108/139 (78%), VIP: 40/62 (65%), FEF: 45/57 (79%).
claims.source: Many central neurons had significant position contributions (Figure 10A,B, filled symbols and bars): OA: 1/27 (4%), VN: 41/49 (84%), CN: 47/61 (77%), PIVC: 63/115 (55%), VPS: 51/69 (74%), MSTd: 108/139 (78%), VIP: 40/62 (65%), FEF: 45/57 (79%).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of neurons with significant position responses across brain regions.

claims.claim: The position contribution was larger in MSTd compared to PIVC and VIP.
claims.source: In agreement with the findings of Chen et al. (2011c), the position contribution was larger in MSTd, as compared to PIVC and VIP (areas for which the distribution is significantly different from MSTd are indicated by stars; *p<0.01; **p<0.001; two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnoff tests).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports statistically significant differences in position contributions between cortical areas.

claims.claim: Central neurons encode jerk (the derivative of linear acceleration) as well as position (displacement).
claims.source: Furthermore, central neurons also encode jerk (the derivative of linear acceleration), as well as position (displacement).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The observed increase in velocity contribution to the spatio-temporal properties of central cells was accompanied by the presence of non-linearities.
claims.source: The observed increase in velocity contribution to the spatio-temporal properties of central cells, as compared to otolith afferents, was accompanied by the presence of non-linearities.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The linear acceleration component of central cells continued to be mostly cosine-tuned like otolith afferents.
claims.source: Whereas the linear acceleration component of central cells continued to be, like otolith afferents, mostly cosine-tuned, the velocity component included substantial omni-directional contributions, and jerk had intermediate properties.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The velocity component of central cells included substantial omni-directional contributions.
claims.source: Whereas the linear acceleration component of central cells continued to be, like otolith afferents, mostly cosine-tuned, the velocity component included substantial omni-directional contributions, and jerk had intermediate properties.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Central neurons carry information about the direction of linear acceleration and also encode the presence or absence of translational motion without regard for direction.
claims.source: Thus, central neurons, like afferents, continued to carry information about the direction of linear acceleration, but they also encoded another type of signal: the presence or absence of translational motion without regard for direction.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The omnidirectional motion signal in central neurons cannot be characterized with steady-state sinusoidal stimuli.
claims.source: This component, which was strong in both the cortex and vestibular/cerebellar nuclei, cannot be characterized with the steady-state sinusoidal stimuli that have traditionally been the stimuli of choice in the vestibular system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: There were only moderate differences in the relative contributions of velocity, acceleration and jerk among central subcortical and cortical neurons.
claims.source: In contrast to the large differences in the types of signals encoded by otolith afferents versus their target cells in the vestibular nuclei, we found only moderate differences in the relative contributions of velocity, acceleration and jerk among central subcortical (vestibular and cerebellar nuclei) and cortical neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Response amplitude to an identical stimulus was lowest in otolith afferents and greatest in vestibular/cerebellar nuclei, PIVC and VPS.
claims.source: Furthermore, response amplitude to an identical stimulus was lowest in otolith afferents and greatest in vestibular/cerebellar nuclei, PIVC and VPS – the areas known to form the core of the central vestibular system (Angelaki et al., 2009; Lopez and Blanke, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Response amplitude is lower in MSTd, VIP and FEF, which are visual/vestibular multisensory areas.
claims.source: In contrast, response amplitude is lower in MSTd, VIP and FEF, which are visual/vestibular multisensory areas.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The signal transformation between sensory afferents and their targets in the brainstem and cerebellum represents a key processing element in the vestibular system.
claims.source: In summary, these results suggest that the signal transformation that takes place between sensory afferents and their targets in the brainstem and cerebellum represents a key processing element in the vestibular system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Using identical passive stimuli, cortical areas show moderate differences compared to the response properties in the brainstem and cerebellum.
claims.source: Using identical passive stimuli, cortical areas show moderate differences, as compared to the response properties in the brainstem and cerebellum.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Afferents from a single otolith organ differ in both spatial and temporal response properties.
claims.source: First, afferents from a single otolith organ differ in both spatial and temporal response properties (Fernández and Goldberg, 1976a, 1976b, 1976c; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Yu et al., 2012; Jamali et al., 2013) and extensive convergence in the vestibular nuclei (Kushiro et al., 2000; Straka et al., 2002; Uchino et al., 2001; Uchino and Kushiro, 2011) creates complex spatio-temporal convergence properties (Angelaki et al., 1992; Bush et al., 1993; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Dickman and Angelaki, 2002; Chen-Huang and Peterson, 2006, 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement summarizes established knowledge from prior literature about otolith afferent properties.

claims.claim: Otolith afferents cannot distinguish tilt relative to gravity from translational acceleration.
claims.source: Second, otolith afferents cannot distinguish tilt relative to gravity from translational acceleration.
claims.evidence: This statement describes a fundamental property of otolith afferents based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: The tilt/translation ambiguity has been resolved in the cortex, where neurons selective for inertial (translational) accelerations are found in PIVC and MSTd.
claims.source: However, this tilt/translation ambiguity has been resolved in the cortex, where neurons that are selective for inertial (translational) accelerations are found (PIVC: Liu et al., 2011; MSTd: Liu and Angelaki, 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement cites prior work showing resolution of the tilt/translation ambiguity in cortex.

claims.claim: The property of cortical neurons being selective for inertial accelerations is likely inherited from subcortical signals through otolith/canal convergence in the brainstem and cerebellum.
claims.source: This property of cortical neurons is likely inherited from subcortical signals, as there is growing evidence that this computation is implemented through otolith/canal convergence in the brainstem and cerebellum (VN/CN: Angelaki et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2013; caudal cerebellar vermis: Yakusheva et al., 2007; Laurens et al., 2013a, 2013b).
claims.evidence: This statement cites evidence for the neural mechanisms underlying tilt/translation disambiguation.

claims.claim: It is possible that the large differences in spatio-temporal response properties between otolith afferents and VN/CN neurons arise from neural computations that resolve the tilt/translation ambiguity.
claims.source: It is thus possible that the large differences in spatio-temporal response properties that we have found between otolith afferents and VN/CN neurons arise from neural computations that resolve the tilt/translation ambiguity, a vital and critically important function for spatial orientation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Otolith afferents have been previously characterized in terms of preferred direction in three-dimensions and response dynamics.
claims.source: Otolith afferents have been previously characterized in terms of preferred direction in three-dimensions (Fernández and Goldberg, 1976a; Tomko et al., 1981; Yu et al., 2012) and response dynamics (Anderson et al., 1978; Fernández and Goldberg, 1976b; Goldberg et al., 1990; Si et al., 1997; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Purcell et al., 2003; Jamali et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement summarizes prior literature on otolith afferent characterization.

claims.claim: The activity of each otolith afferent fiber is determined by the product of a temporal 'transfer' function and a cosine-tuned spatial function.
claims.source: These two properties are separable, with the activity of each afferent fiber being determined by the product of a temporal 'transfer' function and a cosine-tuned spatial function (Fernández and Goldberg, 1976a, 1976b, 1976c).
claims.evidence: This statement cites prior work establishing the separability of spatial and temporal properties in otolith afferents.

claims.claim: Otolith afferents have the same response dynamics along different spatial directions as a result of spatio-temporal separability.
claims.source: As a result of this separability, otolith afferents have the same response dynamics along different spatial directions.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the separability property.

claims.claim: Otolith afferents differ in their response dynamics based upon the regularity of their spontaneous discharge.
claims.source: It has long been recognized that otolith afferents differ in their response dynamics based upon the regularity of their spontaneous discharge (Anderson et al., 1978; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Blanks and Precht, 1978; Fernández and Goldberg, 1976b, 1976c; Goldberg et al., 1990; Jamali et al., 2009, 2013; Purcell et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This statement summarizes established knowledge from prior literature.

claims.claim: The most regular otolith afferents encoded pure acceleration, whereas more irregular afferents encoded mixtures of acceleration and jerk.
claims.source: Thus, the most regular afferents encoded pure acceleration, whereas more irregular afferents encoded mixtures of acceleration and jerk.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claims.claim: The findings of phase leads and gain advances in less regularly-firing afferents are consistent with previous studies using sinusoidal stimulation.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with previous studies reporting phase leads and gain advances in less regularly-firing afferents during sinusoidal stimulation (Anderson et al., 1978; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Fernández and Goldberg, 1976b; Goldberg et al., 1990; Jamali et al., 2013; Purcell et al., 2003; Si et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This statement relates the current findings to prior literature.

claims.claim: Less regular-firing otolith afferents included a small but consistent velocity component whose preferred direction relative to jerk and acceleration components is correlated with CV*.
claims.source: Less regular-firing afferents also included a small but consistent velocity component, whose preferred direction relative to that of the jerk and acceleration components is correlated with CV*.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a novel finding from the current study.

claims.claim: The velocity component in less regular-firing afferents has not been described previously using sinusoidal stimulation.
claims.source: Such a response component has not been described previously using sinusoidal stimulation.
claims.evidence: This statement indicates the novelty of the velocity component finding.

claims.claim: VN neurons receive extensive convergence from otolith afferents that vary in their 3D spatial and temporal properties.
claims.source: Because VN neurons receive extensive convergence from otolith afferents that vary in their 3D spatial and temporal properties, a computational challenge arises.
claims.evidence: This statement describes the anatomical basis for the computational challenge.

claims.claim: Theoretical analysis showed that central neurons receiving otolith afferent convergence should exhibit spatio-temporal convergence properties where spatial and temporal coding might not necessarily be separable.
claims.source: Theoretical analysis of such convergence showed that central neurons receiving otolith afferent convergence should, in general, exhibit spatio-temporal convergence properties, where spatial and temporal coding might not necessarily be separable; this results in complex spatial (non-cosine-tuned) properties, where central neurons carry different proportions of velocity, acceleration and jerk signals along different spatial directions (Angelaki, 1992a, 1992b, 1992c; Schor and Angelaki, 1992; Angelaki et al., 1993; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000).
claims.evidence: This statement cites prior theoretical work predicting non-separable properties in central neurons.

claims.claim: Evidence for simultaneous coding of both translational acceleration and jerk was demonstrated in VN responses of decerebrate rodents.
claims.source: Evidence for simultaneous coding of both translational acceleration and jerk was indeed demonstrated in VN responses of decerebrate rodents (Angelaki et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This statement cites prior experimental evidence supporting the theoretical predictions.

claims.claim: Some experimental evidence for spatio-temporal convergence properties was provided for neurons in the primate VN and CN.
claims.source: It took several more years until some experimental evidence for spatio-temporal convergence properties was provided for neurons in the primate VN (Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Chen-Huang and Peterson, 2006, 2010) and CN (Shaikh et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement cites prior experimental work on primate VN and CN neurons.

claims.claim: All previously published studies of responses of VN/CN neurons to translation used sinusoidal stimuli.
claims.source: However, to our knowledge, all previously published studies of responses of VN/CN neurons to translation used sinusoidal stimuli.
claims.evidence: This statement characterizes the limitations of prior experimental approaches.

claims.claim: VN and CN responses are characterized by non-minimum phase properties, complicating identification of temporal dynamics using sinusoids.
claims.source: First, VN and CN responses are characterized by non-minimum phase properties, i.e., phase and gain changes do not parallel each other, thus complicating identification of temporal dynamics using sinusoids (Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Dickman and Angelaki, 2002; Shaikh et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement cites prior work identifying limitations of sinusoidal stimuli for characterizing VN/CN responses.

claims.claim: Responses proportional to the temporal derivative and integral of translational acceleration cannot be easily separated using sinusoidal stimuli.
claims.source: Second, responses proportional to the temporal derivative and integral of translational acceleration cannot be easily separated using sinusoidal stimuli (e.g., a phase difference of 90° relative to acceleration could reflect either velocity coding in one direction or jerk coding in the opposite direction).
claims.evidence: This statement explains a fundamental limitation of sinusoidal stimuli.

claims.claim: The traditional approach of testing sinusoidal responses at different frequencies to distinguish velocity from jerk contributions is complicated by non-minimum phase properties.
claims.source: The traditional approach of testing sinusoidal responses at different frequencies to distinguish velocity from jerk contributions using linear systems analyses is complicated by the presence of non-minimum phase properties, thus making system identification challenging (Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Dickman and Angelaki, 2002; Shaikh et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement explains why traditional frequency analysis approaches are problematic for VN/CN neurons.

claims.claim: If response dynamics vary with stimulus direction, a complete characterization of spatio-temporal properties requires testing cells at multiple frequencies and multiple directions in 3D.
claims.source: Furthermore, if indeed response dynamics vary with stimulus direction, a complete characterization of the spatio-temporal properties requires testing cells at multiple frequencies and multiple directions in 3D (Chen-Huang and Peterson, 2006, 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement cites prior work that attempted comprehensive 3D characterization using sinusoids.

claims.claim: Non-linearities in spatio-temporal tuning can violate the assumptions of traditional linear systems analysis.
claims.source: Third, non-linearities in spatio-temporal tuning, as reported here (see also Chen et al., 2011c; Massot et al., 2012) can violate the assumptions of traditional linear systems analysis, thus rendering previous conclusions based on steady-state frequency analysis problematic.
claims.evidence: This statement explains how non-linearities limit the validity of prior approaches.

claims.claim: These limitations have been circumvented by the use of 3D transient stimuli and comparison of neural responses in multiple subcortical and cortical areas.
claims.source: These limitations have been circumvented here, for the first time, by the use of 3D transient stimuli and a comparison of neural responses in multiple subcortical and cortical areas.
claims.evidence: This statement describes the methodological innovation of the current study.

claims.claim: With the exception of Chen-Huang and Peterson (2010), nothing is known about spatio-temporal convergence in any brain region using transient stimuli.
claims.source: With the exception of Chen-Huang and Peterson (2010), who characterized 3D responses in the VN using sinusoidal stimuli (see limitations above), nothing is known about spatio-temporal convergence in any brain region using transient stimuli.
claims.evidence: This statement emphasizes the novelty of the current approach.

claims.claim: Understanding the full extent of underlying spatio-temporal computations is only achievable when data are analyzed in 3D.
claims.source: Yet, as previously also emphasized by Chen-Huang and Peterson (2010), understanding the full extent of the underlying spatio-temporal computations is only achievable when data are analyzed in 3D, and conclusions drawn by characterizing responses along a single direction or within a single plane can be rather incomplete.
claims.evidence: This statement emphasizes the importance of 3D analysis, citing prior work.

claims.claim: The current findings provide the first quantification of 3D spatio-temporal convergence properties using transient stimuli along many spatial directions.
claims.source: Our current findings have provided the first such quantification of 3D spatio-temporal convergence properties using transient stimuli along many spatial directions.
claims.evidence: This statement emphasizes the novelty and significance of the current study.

claims.claim: Most central cells show omni-directional tuning components.
claims.source: Most central cells show omni-directional tuning components.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a key finding about central neuron responses.

claims.claim: The existence of broad or uniform tuning suggests that many afferents converge onto one central neuron.
claims.source: The existence of broad or uniform tuning, as opposed to cosine tuning, suggests that many afferents converge onto one central neuron.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the broad tuning findings.

claims.claim: Broadly tuned neurons respond to motion in directions that are orthogonal to their preferred direction.
claims.source: Indeed, broadly tuned neurons respond to motion in directions that are orthogonal to their PD.
claims.evidence: This statement describes a characteristic of broadly tuned neurons.

claims.claim: In otolith afferents, all directions that are orthogonal to the preferred direction are null directions.
claims.source: In contrast, in OA, all directions that are orthogonal to the PD are null directions.
claims.evidence: This statement describes a characteristic of otolith afferent tuning.

claims.claim: The transformation of responses from sensory afferents to brainstem neurons may be coupled to the resolution of the tilt/translation ambiguity.
claims.source: These results suggest that the transformation of responses from sensory afferents to brainstem neurons represents a key processing element, possibly because it is coupled to the resolution of a tilt/translation ambiguity that represents a critically important function for spatial orientation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Theoretical solutions to the tilt/translation ambiguity problem require strong non-linearities.
claims.source: Although there is no direct evidence yet for such a link, theoretical solutions to the ambiguity problem require strong non-linearities (Borah et al., 1988; Merfeld, 1995; Glasauer and Merfeld, 1997; Merfeld et al., 1999; Angelaki et al., 1999, 2004; Laurens and Droulez, 2007; Laurens and Angelaki, 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement cites theoretical work on tilt/translation disambiguation.

claims.claim: Mixed selectivity plays an important computational role by allowing high-dimensional representations that enable a simple linear readout to generate diverse responses.
claims.source: It has been proposed that mixed selectivity plays an important computational role: high-dimensional representations with mixed selectivity allow a simple linear readout to generate a diverse array of potential responses (Fusi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement cites theoretical work on the computational role of mixed selectivity.

claims.claim: Representations based on highly specialized neurons are low dimensional and may preclude a linear readout from generating several responses that depend on multiple task-relevant variables.
claims.source: In contrast, representations based on highly specialized neurons are low dimensional and may preclude a linear readout from generating several responses that depend on multiple task-relevant variables.
claims.evidence: This statement cites theoretical work contrasting specialized versus mixed selectivity representations.

claims.claim: Complex non-linear operations can be performed by simple linear summations of non-linear neurons.
claims.source: Complex non-linear operations can be performed by simple linear summations of non-linear neurons, and in turn linear summation may be easily learned by neuronal networks.
claims.evidence: This statement describes a theoretical principle about neural computation.

claims.claim: A rich variety of non-linearly transformed signals may facilitate the learning of complex computations.
claims.source: Thus, a rich variety of non-linearly transformed signals may facilitate the learning of complex computations.
claims.evidence: This statement presents a theoretical principle about neural computation.

claims.claim: The spatio-temporal transformations in VN/CN might reflect the need to perform non-linear, three-dimensional spatio-temporal operations necessary to implement an internal model of head motion.
claims.source: It is possible that the described spatio-temporal transformations in VN/CN might reflect the need to perform non-linear, three-dimensional spatio-temporal operations necessary to implement an internal model of head motion (Merfeld, 1995; Laurens and Angelaki, 2011), whose influence has been documented in subcortical neurons (Angelaki et al., 2004; Yakusheva et al., 2007; Laurens et al., 2013a, 2013b).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Complex spatio-temporal representations of movement may be passed on to cortical neurons to subserve their respective roles in spatial cognition.
claims.source: Complex spatio-temporal representations of movement may be passed on to cortical (Liu and Angelaki, 2009; Liu et al., 2011) neurons to subserve their respective roles in spatial cognition.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Each movement trajectory consisted of a Gaussian velocity profile with total displacement of 13 cm and peak acceleration of 0.1 g.
claims.source: Each movement trajectory consisted of a Gaussian velocity profile (0.2 s standard deviation) with corresponding biphasic acceleration and triphasic jerk profiles. The total displacement was 13 cm and the peak acceleration was 0.1 g.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the stimulus parameters.

claims.claim: All movements originated from the center of the movement range of the motion platform, and the platform returned to this starting position during the 2 s inter-trial interval.
claims.source: All movements originated from the center of the movement range of the motion platform, and the platform returned to this starting position during the 2 s inter-trial interval.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental protocol.

claims.claim: Otolith afferents, VN, CN and PIVC neurons are not sensitive to visual stimuli or eye movements.
claims.source: Previous findings have established that otolith afferents, VN, CN and PIVC neurons are not sensitive to visual stimuli or eye movements (for details see Bryan and Angelaki, 2009; Liu et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement cites prior work establishing the lack of visual/eye movement sensitivity in these neurons.

claims.claim: For MSTd, VPS, VIP and FEF neurons, vestibular translation responses during fixation are similar to those in complete darkness.
claims.source: For MSTd, VPS, VIP and FEF neurons, which are sensitive to eye movements and/or visual motion, we have previously verified that vestibular translation responses during fixation are similar to those in complete darkness (details and comparison figures can be found in: Gu et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2007 and Chowdhury et al., 2009 for MSTd, Chen et al., 2011a for VPS, Chen et al., 2011b for VIP and Gu et al., 2016 for FEF).
claims.evidence: This statement cites prior work verifying that vestibular responses are similar in darkness and during fixation.

results.result: The study used a well-defined experimental protocol with 26 directions of 3D translation (45° increments in azimuth and elevation), Gaussian velocity profiles (13 cm displacement, 0.1 g peak acceleration), and analyzed 579 neurons across 8 brain regions from 19 monkeys.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C90-C91 provide comprehensive methodological details about the stimulus design, neural data collection, and sample sizes. The experimental protocol is clearly described with specific quantitative parameters, and the data set composition is explicitly stated with neuron counts per region.

results.result: The VAJ model provided good fits to neural responses (median R² 0.59-0.78 across regions), with otolith afferents best fit by acceleration-only or acceleration+jerk models (48% A, 33% AJ), while central neurons predominantly required the full VAJ model (60%) with velocity as the dominant component.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C16 report quantitative model fitting results with confidence intervals and partial R² values. The distribution of best-fitting models and component contributions are clearly documented, showing a fundamental transformation from peripheral to central processing.

results.result: Otolith afferents exhibit spatially aligned, cosine-tuned responses to acceleration and jerk with high separability (median 0.98), where regular afferents encode pure acceleration while irregular afferents encode acceleration+jerk mixtures correlated with CV*.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C21, C26, C32, C60 collectively demonstrate the spatio-temporal separability of otolith afferents with quantitative evidence (7° median angular difference, separability index 0.98). The relationship between firing regularity and temporal dynamics is well-documented with statistical support.

results.result: Otolith afferent response dynamics vary with firing regularity (CV*): irregular afferents (median CV* 0.06) have higher acceleration and jerk weights than regular afferents (median CV* 0.026, p=10⁻³), with a small velocity component whose preferred direction correlates with CV*.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18, C20, C62 report statistically significant relationships between CV* and response components (p<10⁻²). The novel finding of a velocity component in irregular afferents is supported by correlation analysis, though its magnitude is small (median 0.06).

results.result: Central neurons (VN/CN and cortex) exhibit non-linear mixed selectivity with dissimilar spatial tuning across velocity, acceleration, and jerk components, showing significantly lower separability (median 0.89, p<10⁻¹²) than otolith afferents, with velocity responses dominated by omnidirectional components while acceleration remains mostly cosine-tuned.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C22-C23, C27-C28, C41-C43 provide converging evidence for the transformation from peripheral to central processing. Statistical comparisons show highly significant differences (p<10⁻⁸ to p<10⁻¹⁴) in component weights and separability between otolith afferents and central neurons.

results.result: Among central neurons, VN and CN show similar properties with no significant differences in component weights (p>0.28), while cortical areas show only moderate differences, with visual/vestibular multisensory areas (MSTd, VPS, VIP, FEF) having slightly greater velocity weights (median 0.39) than non-multisensory areas (median 0.32, p<10⁻⁹).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25, C46, C50 demonstrate that the major transformation occurs at the first synapse (afferents to VN/CN), with more modest changes across central areas. Statistical tests support the similarity between VN/CN and the small but significant differences between cortical area types.

results.result: Response amplitude and baseline firing rate vary systematically across the vestibular hierarchy: otolith afferents have the smallest modulation (median 10 spk/s) but highest baseline (72 spk/s), VN/CN/PIVC have the largest modulation (58 spk/s) with intermediate baseline (45 spk/s), and multisensory cortical areas have moderate modulation (35 spk/s) with low baseline (12 spk/s).
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 report highly significant differences (p<10⁻¹¹ to p<10⁻¹³) in response properties across brain regions with clear confidence intervals. The systematic progression from high baseline/low modulation in afferents to low baseline/high modulation in central areas is well-documented.

results.result: Central neurons encode position (displacement) in addition to velocity, acceleration, and jerk, with 55-84% of central neurons showing significant position contributions compared to only 4% of otolith afferents, and MSTd showing larger position contributions than PIVC and VIP.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 report position responses across brain regions, but the authors explicitly note in the Methods that position responses require longer pre- and post-stimulus recording periods for reliable quantification. The PVAJ model analysis is presented but acknowledged as preliminary, limiting confidence in these findings.

results.result: The first synapse (otolith afferents to VN/CN) represents a key processing element that transforms cosine-tuned acceleration signals into mixed selectivity responses encoding both directional information and omnidirectional motion presence, which cannot be characterized with traditional sinusoidal stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C44-C45, C49, C78-C81 present the main conclusion supported by the comprehensive data showing dramatic transformation at the first synapse. The omnidirectional tuning components (broad responses orthogonal to PD) are well-documented and represent a fundamental difference from afferent cosine tuning.

results.result: Prior literature established that otolith afferents are cosine-tuned with separable spatio-temporal properties encoding acceleration, varying in dynamics based on firing regularity, and cannot distinguish tilt from translation, while theoretical work predicted non-separable convergence properties in central neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C51-C52, C56-C59 accurately summarize established knowledge from cited literature. The citations are appropriate and the characterization of prior work on otolith afferent properties and theoretical predictions is consistent with the referenced studies.

results.result: The observed spatio-temporal transformations may be linked to resolution of the tilt/translation ambiguity through otolith/canal convergence in VN/CN, as cortical neurons selective for inertial acceleration likely inherit this property from subcortical processing, and theoretical solutions require strong non-linearities.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55, C82-C83, C88 present speculative interpretations linking the observed transformations to tilt/translation disambiguation. While the citations to prior work are appropriate and the hypothesis is plausible, the authors explicitly state there is 'no direct evidence yet for such a link' (C83), making this interpretation uncertain.

results.result: The current study overcomes limitations of prior sinusoidal stimulation approaches (non-minimum phase properties, inability to separate velocity from jerk, requirement for multi-frequency testing) by using 3D transient stimuli, providing the first comprehensive quantification of spatio-temporal convergence properties across multiple brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C61, C63, C68-C77 accurately characterize limitations of prior approaches and justify the methodological innovation. The novelty claim is supported by appropriate citations, and the advantages of transient stimuli over sinusoidal approaches for characterizing non-linear, non-separable responses are well-articulated.

results.result: Mixed selectivity in central neurons may facilitate complex computations by enabling high-dimensional representations that allow simple linear readouts to generate diverse responses, potentially supporting spatial cognition in cortical areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87, C89 cite theoretical work on mixed selectivity (Fusi et al., 2016) and speculate about functional implications. While the theoretical framework is appropriately cited, the connection to the observed vestibular transformations remains speculative without direct experimental evidence linking mixed selectivity to specific computational functions.

results.result: Response amplitude is highest in vestibular/cerebellar nuclei and PIVC/VPS (core vestibular areas) and lower in visual/vestibular multisensory areas (MSTd, VIP, FEF), consistent with a hierarchical processing pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 report systematic differences in response amplitude across brain regions with appropriate statistical support and citations to prior work characterizing the core vestibular system. The interpretation is consistent with the quantitative data presented in C29-C30.

results.result: Control experiments from prior studies verified that otolith afferents, VN, CN, and PIVC neurons are not sensitive to visual stimuli or eye movements, and that vestibular responses in MSTd, VPS, VIP, and FEF during fixation are similar to those in complete darkness.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 cite multiple prior publications that established these control conditions. The citations are specific and appropriate, providing confidence that visual and eye movement confounds were adequately controlled across the different neuron types studied.

results.result: Prior theoretical work predicted non-separable spatio-temporal convergence in central neurons receiving otolith afferent input, with experimental evidence demonstrated in rodent VN and later in primate VN and CN using sinusoidal stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 accurately summarize the progression of theoretical predictions and experimental validation in prior literature. The citations are appropriate and the characterization of this prior work provides important context for the current findings.
